sourceObservations.observations: Title identifies Lecture 24, The Control Problem for Manipulators, printed page 1. No technical claim.
Contents list manipulator control, feedforward nonlinear control, dual-rate computed torque, parameter ignorance, industrial joint control and Lyapunov analysis. Roadmap only.

Two-link illustration labels inertia coupling M(theta), Coriolis/centrifugal V(theta,thetadot), gravity G(theta), joint torques and downward link weights. Rigid-body equation tau=M qdd+V+G; the text also names friction but it is added explicitly on the next slide. Geometry drawing does not provide numerical mass locations.

Plant includes F(theta,thetadot), explicitly friction/non-rigid-body effects. Partitioned controller tau=alpha*tauprime+beta chooses alpha=M and beta=V+G+F. Exact matched cancellation yields M qdd=M tauprime; invertible M gives qdd=tauprime.

Servo tauprime=qdd_d+Kv Edot+Kp E, E=q_d-q. Exact error equation Edd+Kv Edot+Kp E=0. Joint-wise scalar form needs diagonal gains in original coordinates, not merely invertible or diagonal M. Diagram places sum of feedforward acceleration and both feedback terms before M; V+G+F added afterward. Measured theta supplies M and dynamic compensation; measured velocity enters the latter.

Ideal laws assume continuous computation, exact model knowledge and no sensing/actuation delay. Practical categories are computation time and model inaccuracy; parameters change with load, wear, friction and uncertainty. A changed payload with other conditions fixed directly implicates dynamic-parameter mismatch, not unchanged encoder/timing errors.

Digital sensors and commands operate at discrete instants. Sampling introduces delay/approximation and can degrade tracking/stability when too slow. Fast sampling makes a continuous approximation more reasonable, not automatically exact or stable for any gains/delays.

Paired diagrams distinguish full computed torque with measured-state M and V+G+F from desired-state dynamic feedforward plus direct Kp E and Kv Edot torque corrections. The right dynamic model receives desired position, velocity, acceleration, not actual-state feedback. Moving model computation outside the servo enables precomputation; feedback errors remain measured online.

Printed homogeneous equation is Edd+M^-1 Kv Edot+M^-1 Kp E=0. For the actual desired-state feedforward diagram, the omitted residual is M(q)qdd_d+h(q,qd)-tau_ff; homogeneous form needs this residual zero or neglected. Diagonal physical gains do not generally decouple full inverse inertia. Pole changes mean frozen-configuration models; a moving time-varying trajectory need not have one LTI pole set.

Dual rate assigns expensive nonlinear dynamic calculations to a slower background process and servo feedback/error correction to a faster loop. This is computational scheduling, not automatic parameter identification; held model coefficients can become stale while measured errors update rapidly.

Actual diagram marks B(theta)+C(theta) and G(theta) as background computations. Measured velocity connects into the right of B+C; measured position enters it through a dashed path and enters G. Desired position/velocity only form errors. The page does not separately define B and C formulas despite position-only labels; do not invent their friction or Coriolis assignment.

Disturbance tau_d enters the arm-input summer with a minus sign. Thus actual acceleration includes -M^-1 tau_d and desired-minus-actual error gets +M^-1 tau_d. The equilibrium expression is E=Kp^-1 M^-1 tau_d, in that order, not a universal instantaneous response. Listed examples are payload variation, external forces, friction changes, vibration and unmodeled dynamics. Off-diagonal inverse inertia can couple errors but does not force every component nonzero for every disturbance.

Estimated M,V,G,F are distinguished from actual quantities. Printed uncertainty forcing is Mhat^-1[(M-Mhat)qdd+(V-Vhat)+(G-Ghat)+(F-Fhat)], with actual qdd and the estimated inverse outside. This follows by adding/subtracting Mhat qdd in the matched servo equation. A zero residual at an instant can result from cancellation or unexcited parameter errors and does not identify all parameters.

Qualitative industrial-control claims cite computation cost, incomplete parameters and sufficiently good simpler performance, near-independent joints and workspace compromise. Treat these as course assertions, not a present-day market survey or proof of exact decoupling.

PID slide sets alpha=I,beta=0, diagonal Kp,Kv,Ki, no model compensation, and desired acceleration often omitted because unavailable. The encoder returns measured position to negative comparison input; common error feeds all three PID branches. Adding physical acceleration directly to an SI torque requires inertia-like scaling or an explicitly normalized model. An unavailable desired-acceleration signal set to zero does not imply actual acceleration is zero.

Without decoupling, joints influence one another and rejection is imperfect; fixed gains are an average workspace compromise, not identical damping at every inertia. Estimated gravity is added to improve holding accuracy. The claim gravity creates steady-state error needs qualification with integral action, saturation and model accuracy; it is not an unconditional theorem for an ideal stable PID.

Energy-like analysis can establish stability without solving the differential equation, but stability is not performance. Informal settling wording is overbroad: Lyapunov stability alone is nearby-state containment, not convergence or a settling-time guarantee.

Unforced m*xdd+b*xd+k*x=0, energy v=.5*m*xd^2+.5*k*x^2; vdot=xd*(m*xdd+k*x)=-b*xd^2. With positive m,k,b, energy is positive definite and proper, but vdot is only semidefinite. At instantaneous xd=0, x need not vanish; persistent xd=0 also forces xdd=0 and k*x=0. b=0 conserves energy; k=0 removes positive definiteness in the full state.

Classical direct-method statement requires continuous first partial derivatives, positive definite v with v(0)=0, and vdot<=0; strict negative derivative away from equilibrium gives asymptotic stability under local regularity. The intuition that decreasing energy prevents any unbounded state requires suitable compact sublevels/properness. Positive definiteness is distinct from C1 regularity: absolute-value candidate can fail the latter.

Normalized nonlinear spring-damper xdd+b(xd)+k(x)=0, with xd*b(xd)>0 for nonzero velocity and x*k(x)>0 for nonzero position. Candidate v=.5*xd^2+integral_0^x k(lambda)dlambda. For negative x the integrand and integration orientation both reverse, so the potential remains positive. Continuity/sign conditions at zero matter for equilibrium; the general equilibrium equation before those restrictions is b(0)+k(0)=0.

Differentiation correctly cancels the restoring term and gives vdot=-xd*b(xd). The note distinguishes instantaneous xd=0 from x=0 and motivates the invariant-set check. Its later “for all trajectories” wording must be scoped to trajectories remaining in zero dissipation; the printed -k*x is linear notation whereas the preceding model requires -k(x). A compact positively invariant region supports the qualified convergence argument, not merely an initially compact set or energy bound with unbounded sublevel.
Summary repeats the control problem, practical considerations, industrial joint laws and linear/nonlinear Lyapunov analysis. No new technical premise.
Reference-only slide cites Craig, Introduction to Robotics, third edition, 2004. No new examinable technical content.
Thank-you closing slide, printed page 24; no technical content.

independentAnswers.reasoning: Subtract the same V+G+F from plant and command to obtain M qdd=M tauprime. With invertible M, qdd=tauprime, not velocity and not the un-inverted torque M tauprime.
The source explicitly labels F as friction/non-rigid-body effects, distinct from M times acceleration, velocity-dependent rigid-body V and gravity G.
The exact error equation has coefficient matrices Kv and Kp after inertia cancellation. Diagonal gains in the original joint coordinates remove cross-coordinate terms; M need not have been diagonal.

The diagram sums desired acceleration and both gain-weighted errors first, multiplies that entire normalized command by measured-state M, then adds V+G+F. Moving feedback after M changes the physical gain meaning.

Only payload changes while geometry, sensing, timing and reference remain fixed. The old load parameters therefore create the directly implicated dynamic-model mismatch; unchanged compensated alternatives do not explain the new difference.
Long dynamic-model evaluation is computation-time burden; a wrong friction coefficient is parameter/model inaccuracy. They are distinct implementation limitations.

Shorter sampling periods can improve a continuous-time approximation; they do not identify mass parameters or remove the need to assess discrete gains and delay. Fresh measurements at each faster cycle require more readings per second.
The slide explicitly permits both poor tracking and affected stability under slow sampling; the error is not restricted to static offsets, command appearance or a time-axis rescaling.

Known desired position, velocity and acceleration permit precomputing the desired-state dynamic torque. Actual future errors cannot be obtained from the reference alone, so measured-error feedback remains online.
Using tau=tau_ff+Kv Edot+Kp E and M qdd+h=tau, multiply Edd=qdd_d-qdd by M: M Edd=M qdd_d+h-tau_ff-Kv Edot-Kp E. Moving gains left leaves M qdd_d+h-tau_ff, with this sign and actual-state arguments.

For a full inverse inertia, right-multiplication by a diagonal gain scales its columns rather than deleting off-diagonal elements. M^-1 Kp and M^-1 Kv can remain coupled and do not generally commute with their gains.

Frozen-configuration coefficient matrices can have different poles as M changes. The moving system is generally time-varying, so initial or average frozen poles are not an exact single global LTI description.

Fast errors can be current while model coefficients are held from an earlier configuration. Sensor reads do not implicitly recompute a background model; stale coefficients affect actual compensation torque.
Tracing the actual arrows: measured theta and thetadot enter the B+C model, while measured theta enters gravity. Desired signals are used in error comparisons, not these shown model inputs.

The page labels a background additive B(theta)+C(theta) path without separate defining equations. Its measured-velocity input is visible despite abbreviated position-only labels. No individual Coriolis, centrifugal or friction formula can be attributed to this page alone.

The diagram subtracts tau_d from commanded torque, hence qdd=tauprime-M^-1 tau_d under exact compensation. Edd=qdd_d-qdd reverses that disturbance contribution, giving positive M^-1 tau_d in the error equation.
Left-multiply Kp E=M^-1 tau_d by Kp^-1. The order is Kp^-1 M^-1 tau_d; swapping the inverse matrices needs an additional commutation condition not given.

The expression is an equilibrium relation with vanishing error derivatives, not an arbitrary instantaneous forced response. Inverse inertia can couple one applied joint disturbance into other errors, but cancellations/zero matrix entries prevent any universal all-components-nonzero claim. Diagonal Kp alone does not remove full inverse inertia.

The five printed examples are payload variation, external forces, friction changes, vibration and unmodeled dynamics. The other lists contain possible implementation imperfections but are not the source enumeration requested.
The residual torque is (3-2)*4+1+2-1=6 N m. The printed prefactor is estimated inverse inertia 1/2, yielding 3 rad/s², not division by actual 3, omission of the inverse, or sign reversal.

A zero combined residual at one instant is weaker than all component models being exact: nonzero terms may cancel, or an inertia error is unexcited when acceleration is zero. It cannot uniquely identify inertia or gravity either.

The lecture gives computation burden, incomplete parameters and sufficient simpler-controller performance as reasons. This is explicitly course-specific qualitative reasoning rather than a current industry census.
The encoder returns measured actual position to the minus input of desired-minus-actual comparison. That common error then branches to proportional, derivative and integral paths.

SI angular acceleration has units rad/s², whereas the command sum is torque. An inertia-like factor with torque per angular acceleration converts it; inverse inertia, proportional torque/angle or damping torque/angular-velocity factors do not. A fully declared normalized-unit model is another consistent interpretation.

The slide omits full compensation via alpha=I,beta=0 and may set an unavailable desired-acceleration input to zero. That implementation omission is not a statement that the specified desired trajectory or actual joint has zero physical acceleration, nor does integral action reconstruct exact dynamics.

With physical fixed gains, inertia/configuration changes alter effective normalized gains and damping. A workspace compromise need not achieve the same damping at every posture; integral action alone does not enforce it.

Lyapunov stability says sufficiently nearby initial states remain nearby. Convergence needs stronger hypotheses, and neither exact settling time nor finite-time arrival follows from mere nonincrease of a candidate.
Differentiate .5*m*xd²+.5*k*x² to get m*xd*xdd+k*x*xd=xd*(m*xdd+k*x). Substitute the plant m*xdd+k*x=-b*xd to obtain -b*xd².
Kinetic energy is .5*2*(-1)²=1 J and potential energy is .5*8*(.5)²=1 J, totaling 2 J. Dissipation rate is -3*(-1)²=-3 W.
With b>0, -b*xd²=0 implies xd=0 at that instant. The plant then gives xdd=-k*x/m, which can be nonzero if displacement is nonzero; zero instantaneous dissipation is not rest equilibrium.

A trajectory remaining at vdot=0 has xd identically zero, hence xdd identically zero. The plant then requires k*x=0 and, with k>0, x=0. Positive quadratic energy gives compact sublevels; this invariant-set step, not instantaneous zero dissipation, supplies convergence.

With b=0, vdot=0 identically. For positive m,k and nonzero initial energy, the harmonic oscillator conserves that energy and does not approach the zero-energy origin. This boundary case is stable but not asymptotically stable.

With k=0, v=.5*m*xd² vanishes at every (x,0), including nonzero x. It is positive definite only in the reduced velocity variable and semidefinite on the full position-velocity state; the sign of displacement is not the issue.

dv/dx=x and xdot=-x³ imply vdot=-x⁴, strictly negative for x nonzero. The C1 positive candidate and smooth equilibrium meet the local strict direct-method test. Differentiating the vector field instead would give -3x², not vdot.
Integrate k(lambda)=lambda+lambda³ from zero to x: x²/2+x⁴/4. The derivative of this potential returns x+x³; squaring force or omitting integration factors is wrong.

At x=1, potential is .5+.25=.75 and kinetic term .5*(-2)²=2, so v=2.75. b(-2)=-4-8=-12 and -xd*b(xd)=-(-2)*(-12)=-24. Omitting the quartic integration factor gives potential1.5, total3.5; using the damping value b(-2) directly instead of multiplying by -xd gives -12.

At a zero-state equilibrium both velocity and acceleration vanish, so the general equation requires b(0)+k(0)=0. Before stronger sign restrictions, the two values may be nonzero opposites; equal nonzero values, derivative conditions or merely one zero value do not suffice.

The fundamental theorem plus chain rule gives vdot=xd*xdd+k(x)*xd. Substituting xdd=-b(xd)-k(x) cancels restoring terms and leaves -xd*b(xd); neither k prime nor a flipped restoring sign belongs in this derivative.

The selected trajectory must remain in a compact positively invariant subset of the domain so its limiting behavior is contained where the derivative and invariant-set hypotheses apply. Initial compactness alone, arbitrary unbounded invariant sets and energy upper bounds with unbounded sublevels do not supply this trajectory compactness.

Both |x1|+x2² and x1²+x2² vanish only at (0,0) and are positive elsewhere. The first has one-sided x1 derivatives -1 and +1 on x1=0 and is not C1 there; the polynomial has continuous first derivatives. Continuity alone is not differentiability, and no system stability is established without its derivative test.
